metaDescription: Six Anker power banks compared by capacity, charging speed, built-in cable and pocket size, so you can match the right model to daily carry or travel.
introParagraphs: Anker sells a long line of power banks, and the names alone make it hard to tell them apart. This guide narrows it to six models that cover the real choices: three 10,000mAh packs for pockets and purses, and three 20,000mAh packs for long trips and shared charging. The spread is wide. The Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 45W can send 40W to an iPhone 17 and 45W to Samsung phones, while the Anker 10,000mAh PowerIQ model sticks to a plain 5V/3A output.

Size and speed pull in opposite directions. The Anker Nano 45W 10,000mAh measures just 3.21 x 1.99 x 1.42 inches and weighs 8.2 oz with a retractable USB-C cable, while the Anker 20,000mAh 87W is built to split power across three ports, with one device receiving up to 65W. Between them sit the Anker 10,000mAh 30W at 4.32 x 2.58 x 0.98 inches, and the two Zolo 20,000mAh versions that differ mainly in wattage, 45W versus 30W.

We evaluated each pick based on product specs and buyer feedback, with an eye on what matters to active adults and the family members buying for them: a built-in cable you cannot forget, an output strong enough for a modern phone, a size that fits a handbag, and a capacity that stays under the airline limit. Every pick here is a 10,000mAh or 20,000mAh unit, so all of them sit comfortably under the 100 Wh cabin threshold.

products.name: Anker Zolo Power Bank 20,000mAh 45W

specList.label: Best for
specList.value: Phone plus tablet or laptop trips

products.description:
The Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 45W is the pick that balances every spec in this lineup. The 20,000mAh cell is described as good for about 3.3 charges of an iPhone 17 Pro or about 3 charges of a Samsung S25 Ultra. The built-in USB-C port and cable run at 40W for an iPhone 17 and up to 45W for Samsung devices, which is the top phone-charging speed in this guide for a single device.

The tradeoff is bulk. A 20,000mAh pack is a real object in a bag, and it will feel heavier than the Nano or the 10,000mAh models. The cable is only 5.98 inches long, so charging a phone while holding it means the phone sits close to the bank, and you will want a separate longer cable for use on a couch or in bed. This is a good fit for someone who travels a few times a year or who wants one charger that also helps a tablet.

Ownership is straightforward because the cable is permanently attached, so there is no cord to lose in a coat pocket. Recharging uses the same USB-C port, so a good wall adapter matters if you want a short refill time. Compared with the Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 30W, you pay for 15 extra watts of output that mainly help Samsung and larger devices, and compared with the 87W model you give up the three-port sharing in exchange for a simpler, lighter design.

products.name: Anker Power Bank 10,000mAh 30W
products.description:
This is the Anker that most people will actually keep in a purse or jacket. At 10,000mAh it is described as delivering about 2 full charges for an iPhone 15 and just under 2 for a comparable Android phone. The 30W output is twice as fast as an older 5V/3A charger, and the listing says an iPhone 16 Pro Max reaches 50% in a short stretch.

The built-in 5.4-inch USB-C cable is rated for over 10,000 bends, which speaks to the weak point of most cheap banks. Its footprint of 4.32 x 2.58 x 0.98 inches makes it thicker than the PowerIQ model, so it feels more like a deck of cards than a slim wallet. The USB-C input also doubles as a way to recharge it, which keeps the cable story simple for someone who owns mostly USB-C devices.

The main limit is that it has fewer ports than the 20,000mAh models, so it is not the choice for sharing power with a spouse on a long day. Against the Anker Nano 45W, it gives up some top speed and the retractable cable but is a bit less expensive in the lineup and similarly easy to use. Against the 5V/3A PowerIQ pack, the 30W output is the reason to step up, since it noticeably shortens the wait when a phone is already low.

products.name: Anker Nano Power Bank 45W 10,000mAh
products.description:
The Anker Nano 45W packs 10,000mAh into a block of just 3.21 x 1.99 x 1.42 inches, and Anker describes it as 16% smaller than standard 10,000mAh packs. It weighs 8.2 oz and includes a built-in retractable USB-C cable, which is the cleanest cable design in the guide because nothing dangles. The smart display shows remaining charge, a feature that is genuinely useful for people who dislike guessing from four tiny lights.

The performance is better than the size suggests. A single USB-C output reaches 45W, enough for phones and for lighter laptops, and the unit accepts up to 30W on input for quick recharges. Pass-through technology lets you charge the bank and a device at once, which is handy on a hotel nightstand where you only have one outlet.

The tradeoff is shape, since the Nano is tall and thick relative to a flat pack and it can poke in a slim pocket. It is also a one-port device, so you cannot charge two phones simultaneously the way you can with the Anker 20,000mAh 87W. Compared with the 10,000mAh 30W model, you pay for the retractable cable, the display, and 15W more output, which suits people who use a tablet or a Samsung phone that benefits from the higher speed.

products.name: Anker Power Bank 20,000mAh 87W
products.description:
The Anker 20,000mAh 87W is the most powerful model here and the only one that is meant to share across three devices. The 87W total can be distributed across ports, with a single device receiving up to 65W. That is enough to charge a MacBook Air to about 52% in 30 minutes, and the listing says an iPhone 15 Pro reaches 58% in the same time through the built-in cable.

That power comes with the heaviest and thickest body in the guide, so it belongs in a travel bag, not a pocket. For a retired couple who share a power bank on a long flight or drive, the three ports are the reason to pick it: a phone, a tablet, and a pair of earbuds can all charge at once. If you only ever charge one phone, you are paying in bulk for headroom you will not use.

Ownership is easy because the built-in cable cannot go missing, but you will need a capable USB-C wall adapter to refill 20,000mAh in a reasonable time. Compared with the Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 45W, this model trades simplicity for 65W single-device power and a third port. Compared with the Nano, it makes more sense if you own a laptop or two devices that regularly drain together.

products.name: Anker Zolo Power Bank 20,000mAh 30W
products.description:
This is the Zolo for people who want large capacity without paying for the fastest output. The 20,000mAh cell is described as covering up to 4 charges of an iPhone 15 and about 3.79 of a Samsung S24, which is more capacity per phone than any other pick in this guide. The 30W output is plenty fast for phones, and the 20W input means a refill takes a reasonable time on a standard adapter.

The design mirrors the more expensive Zolo, with a 5.98-inch built-in USB-C cable meant to withstand repeated use. What you lose is the 45W top speed, so a Samsung phone that can accept higher wattage will charge noticeably slower, and a laptop is a stretch. Weight and size are similar to the 45W version, so the savings are in the electronics, not in the bag.

For most active adults, the trade is sensible. If you mostly charge a phone on trips or during outages, the 30W model does the job and keeps the cost lower. Compared with the Anker 10,000mAh 30W, you double the capacity for a heavier carry, and compared with the Zolo 45W, you accept slower peak charging in exchange for the same runtime and a better price position.

products.name: Anker Power Bank 10,000mAh PowerIQ
products.description:
The PowerIQ 10,000mAh is the slimmest and lowest-priced Anker in this comparison, at 5.99 x 2.81 x 0.61 inches and 8.6 oz. It is described as giving 2 charges for an iPhone 15 and about 1.93 for a similar Android phone, which matches the 30W model on runtime. The body is flat and rectangular, so it slides into a pocket or slim bag more easily than the thicker 30W pack.

The tradeoff is speed and cabling. The output is a plain 5V/3A, which is much slower than the 30W and 45W models, so topping a phone off before leaving the house takes noticeably longer. It also does not have a built-in cable, so you carry your own USB-C cable, and that is the one thing people forget. Anker lists scratch resistance and certification by a 3.2 ft drop test, which is reassuring for a pack that lives in a bag.

It makes sense for a second bank in a glovebox, a nightstand, or a gift for a relative who just wants a safe backup and does not care about speed. Compared with the 30W Anker 10,000mAh, you give up charging speed and the integrated cable, and in return you get a thinner profile and a lower position in the lineup.

buyingCriteria.explanation: mAh is a convenient label but watt-hours are what airlines and fair comparisons use. The formula is mAh divided by 1000 times about 3.6 to 3.7 volts, which makes a 10,000mAh Anker about 37 Wh and a 20,000mAh Anker such as the Zolo 45W about 74 Wh. Both sit well under the 100 Wh cabin limit, so no airline approval is needed. A 30,000mAh pack would land near 108 to 111 Wh and need approval, which is a reason none of these picks go that large. Expect real output to be roughly 77 to 83% of the rated figure, so a 20,000mAh Anker delivers closer to 3 phone charges than the maximum on paper.

Speed comes from watts, not capacity. The Anker PowerIQ pack uses 5V/3A, which is 15W, while the Anker 10,000mAh 30W doubles that and the Zolo 45W reaches 40W for iPhone 17 and 45W for Samsung. USB-C PD spans about 18 to 100W, whereas older USB-A ports sit around 5 to 12W. If you charge a phone at the last minute before leaving, pay for 30W or more. If the bank lives on a nightstand and charges overnight, the slower PowerIQ model is perfectly fine.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Built-in cable vs bring your own
buyingCriteria.explanation: A built-in cable removes the most common failure, which is arriving without one. The Anker Zolo models use a 5.98-inch cable and the Anker 10,000mAh 30W uses a 5.4-inch cable rated for over 10,000 bends. The Nano goes further with a retractable cable that tucks away. The cost is that a short cable keeps the phone close to the bank, and if the cable ever fails you may lose the main port, which is why the PowerIQ model with a removable cable is the more repairable design. Choose built-in if you value never forgetting, and choose removable if you want longevity.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Size and weight in your bag
buyingCriteria.explanation: The most capable bank is useless if you leave it at home because it is heavy. The Anker Nano measures 3.21 x 1.99 x 1.42 inches and weighs 8.2 oz, the 10,000mAh 30W is 4.32 x 2.58 x 0.98 inches, and the PowerIQ is flat at 5.99 x 2.81 x 0.61 inches and 8.6 oz. The 20,000mAh models are bigger still, and the 87W is the heaviest. A good rule is to pick 10,000mAh if you carry it daily and 20,000mAh only for trips, since a daily bank you actually carry beats a better one in a drawer.

Most Ankers here have one main output, which is fine for one person. The Anker 20,000mAh 87W splits power across three ports and delivers up to 65W to a single device, which is the only model that handles a phone, a tablet, and earbuds at once. The Nano has pass-through, letting you charge it while powering a device, which is useful where there is one outlet. Count how many devices you actually charge together, because paying for multi-port power you never use adds weight without benefit.

Look for UL or FCC marks and built-in protection against overcharge and short circuit, which Anker lists across this range. Carry power banks in your cabin bag, not checked luggage, and check that the Wh rating is printed on the unit because security can confiscate a bank without one. Every pick here falls under 100 Wh, so the Zolo 20,000mAh models at about 74 Wh are airline-friendly. Keep it away from heat in a parked car, and replace a bank that swells or runs unusually hot.

howWeEvaluated.title: Capacity versus real use
howWeEvaluated.description: We converted each pack to watt-hours and compared it to the charge counts printed in the listings. The Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 30W sits at the top for phone charges, while the PowerIQ 10,000mAh sits near the bottom with about two. Because usable output is usually 77 to 83% of the rated figure, we treated claimed charge counts as a ceiling, not a promise.

howWeEvaluated.title: Charging speed
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared maximum output wattage and the device each bank is designed to feed. The Zolo 45W at 40W for an iPhone 17 and 45W for Samsung is the fastest phone charger here, while the 5V/3A PowerIQ is the most basic. We also weighed input speed, since a bank that refills slowly is a chore for people who recharge weekly.

howWeEvaluated.title: Cable design and durability
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at whether a cable is built in, how long it is, and what the listing says about bend ratings. The Anker 10,000mAh 30W lists over 10,000 bends, and the Nano's retractable cable avoids tangling. We treated a short built-in cable as a tradeoff rather than a flaw, since it is convenient but limits use while charging.

howWeEvaluated.title: Size, weight and carry comfort
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared dimensions and weight to judge whether each bank fits a handbag, a jacket, or only a travel bag. The Nano at 3.21 x 1.99 x 1.42 inches is the most compact by footprint, the PowerIQ is the thinnest, and the Anker 20,000mAh 87W is the largest. A bank that is comfortable to carry is more valuable than a more powerful one that stays at home.

howWeEvaluated.title: Value and flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each pick by relative price tier and by how many jobs it can do. The PowerIQ is the most affordable entry, the 30W 10,000mAh is a mid-range daily choice, and the 87W is the premium all-purpose option. This is based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on measurements, and the score favors the best balance for an adult carrying one device.

cards.label: 10,000mAh
cards.text: Fits the Anker Nano 45W, the Anker 10,000mAh 30W and the PowerIQ. You get about two phone charges and a bank small enough to carry every day. Recommendation: choose 10,000mAh if you want something you will never leave behind.

cards.label: 20,000mAh
cards.text: Fits the Zolo 45W, the Zolo 30W and the Anker 87W. You get three to four phone charges, tablet support and extra heft. Recommendation: choose 20,000mAh if you travel, lose power at home, or share a bank with a partner.

howToChoose.intro: Pick the speed to match how you charge.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: A printed Wh rating at or under 100 Wh so the bank can ride in a carry-on with no airline approval. Capacity labelled in mAh alone is a red flag, since security can confiscate a bank they cannot verify.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 45W at about 74 Wh is the best fit for flights, with fast charging and a built-in cable that cannot get lost in the seat pocket. The Anker Nano 45W is the better choice if you only need one top-off and want it light.

cards.label: Spend more if
cards.text: You charge a tablet or laptop, share with a partner, or use a Samsung phone that benefits from high wattage. The Anker 20,000mAh 87W and the Zolo 45W earn their price because the extra watts shorten every top-off.

cards.label: Save if
cards.text: You mostly charge one phone and the bank spends most of its time in a drawer or glovebox. The Anker PowerIQ 10,000mAh or the Zolo 20,000mAh 30W cover that need without paying for speed you will not use.

faq.q: Which Anker portable charger should most people buy?
faq.a: For most adults, the Anker Zolo 20,000mAh 45W is the strongest all-round pick because it combines capacity, speed and a built-in cable. If you carry a bank daily, the Anker 10,000mAh 30W is the better fit since it is smaller and still fast enough. The Nano 45W is the right upgrade when you want a display and retractable cable in a compact shell.

faq.q: Can I take these on a plane?
faq.a: Yes. Every pick in this guide is under 100 Wh, which is the cabin limit that needs no airline approval. A 20,000mAh bank is roughly 74 Wh and a 10,000mAh bank about 37 Wh. Always carry it in your cabin bag rather than checked luggage and check your own airline's rules.

faq.q: How many phone charges will I really get?
faq.a: Expect less than the listing's maximum, since usable output is roughly 77 to 83% of the rated capacity. The Zolo 20,000mAh 30W is described as up to 4 charges of an iPhone 15, which in practice is closer to 3. A 10,000mAh Anker is closer to 1.5 to 2 charges.

faq.q: Is a built-in cable better than a separate one?
faq.a: It is more convenient because you cannot forget it, and the Anker Zolo and 30W models use short built-in USB-C cables. The downside is length and repairability, since a damaged built-in cable can end the bank's usefulness. The PowerIQ model has no built-in cable, so it is the one to choose if you prefer to replace cables.

Only if you charge a laptop or several devices at the same time. The Anker 20,000mAh 87W can feed up to 65W to a single device and share across three ports. For one phone, the Zolo 45W or the 30W 10,000mAh gives nearly the same experience in a lighter bag.

faq.q: How do I make a power bank last longer?
faq.a: Avoid leaving it in a hot car, since heat is the fastest way to wear out lithium cells. Recharge it every few months if it sits in a drawer, and use a decent wall adapter so it refills at the rated input. Stop using any bank that swells, gets unusually hot or smells odd.

faq.q: Does charging speed matter if I only charge overnight?
faq.a: Not much. A slow 5V/3A bank like the Anker PowerIQ fills a phone fine overnight, and it costs less. Speed matters when you charge in a rush, such as before leaving the house or at an airport gate, where 30W or 45W models save real time.
